body_html:
Spanish for online meetings is its own small language. Video calls with colleagues in Mexico City, clients in Bogotá or a team in Madrid follow the same structure as in English, but the polite formulas are different, and the tech vocabulary changes by country. Spanish work culture also tends to start with a little small talk and to soften interruptions more than many American teams do. Here are the phrases for each stage of a call, from the first ¿me escuchan bien? to the final que tengan buen día.

Quick answer
  • Opening: Buenos días a todos. ¿Me escuchan bien?
  • Problems: Creo que tienes el micrófono apagado.
  • Interrupting: Perdón que interrumpa, pero…
  • Closing: Entonces, quedamos así. ¡Gracias a todos!
{{toc}}

Spanish for online meetings: opening the call

SpanishEnglish
Buenos días a todos.Good morning, everyone.
¿Me escuchan bien?Can you all hear me okay?
Vamos a esperar un par de minutos a que se conecten todos.Let’s wait a couple of minutes for everyone to join.
Gracias por conectarse.Thanks for joining.
El objetivo de hoy es…Today’s goal is…
Tenemos treinta minutos, así que vamos al grano.We have thirty minutes, so let’s get to the point.

A minute of small talk at the start is normal and appreciated: ¿Cómo va todo por allá? (How’s everything there?) ¿Qué tal el fin de semana? Jumping straight into business can feel cold to Latin American colleagues.

Audio, video and screen sharing

SpanishEnglish
Estás en silencio.You’re on mute.
Creo que tienes el micrófono apagado.I think your microphone is off.
Se te escucha entrecortado.You’re breaking up.
Se congeló la pantalla.The screen froze.
¿Ven mi pantalla?Can you see my screen?
Voy a compartir mi pantalla.I’m going to share my screen.
Te paso el enlace por el chat.I’ll send you the link in the chat.
Se me fue el internet.My internet went out.

You will also hear plenty of English: el link, hacer mute, compartir el screen. In relaxed teams this is normal; in formal meetings, the Spanish versions above sound more professional. The Fundéu foundation suggests Spanish alternatives for many tech terms.

{{image:2}}

Taking turns and interrupting politely

  • Perdón que interrumpa, pero… Sorry to interrupt, but…
  • ¿Puedo agregar algo? Can I add something?
  • Adelante. Go ahead.
  • Perdón, hablamos al mismo tiempo. Sigue tú. Sorry, we talked at the same time. You go.
  • Me gustaría escuchar la opinión de Laura. I’d like to hear Laura’s opinion.
  • Retomando lo que dijo Carlos… Going back to what Carlos said…

With delays on video calls, people often talk over each other. A quick perdón, sigue tú keeps the meeting friendly.

Agreeing, disagreeing and asking for clarification

  • Estoy de acuerdo. I agree.
  • Tiene sentido. That makes sense.
  • Entiendo el punto, pero tengo una duda. I see the point, but I have a question.
  • No estoy del todo convencido. I’m not completely convinced.
  • ¿Me lo podrías explicar otra vez? Could you explain it again?
  • A ver si entendí bien: … Let me check I understood: …

Disagreeing directly can sound blunt in Spanish business culture, especially in Mexico. Acknowledge the other view first; see {{link:disagreeing-politely-in-spanish|disagreeing politely in Spanish}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Closing the meeting and next steps

SpanishEnglish
Para resumir…To sum up…
Los siguientes pasos son…The next steps are…
¿Quién se encarga de esto?Who will take care of this?
Yo me encargo.I’ll take care of it.
Les mando un resumen por correo.I’ll send you a summary by email.
Entonces, quedamos así.So, that’s what we’ve agreed.
Gracias a todos por su tiempo.Thank you all for your time.
Que tengan buen día.Have a good day, everyone.

For the follow-up email, see {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.

A sample meeting opening

Andrea: Buenos días a todos. ¿Me escuchan bien?
Good morning, everyone. Can you hear me okay?

Jorge: Sí, perfecto. Pero no te vemos, creo que tienes la cámara apagada.
Yes, perfectly. But we can’t see you; I think your camera is off.

Andrea: ¡Ay, perdón! ¿Ahora sí?
Oops, sorry! How about now?

Jorge: Ahora sí. ¿Empezamos?
Now we can. Shall we start?

Andrea: Sí. El objetivo de hoy es revisar el calendario del proyecto. Voy a compartir mi pantalla.
Yes. Today’s goal is to review the project calendar. I’m going to share my screen.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • ¿Pueden oírme? Correct, but ¿Me escuchan bien? is what people say on calls.
  • Vamos a tener una reunión online. Fine in speech, but in writing, en línea or virtual is more standard.
  • Using tú with a new client. Start with usted and follow their lead. See {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.
  • Estoy excitado por el proyecto. This sounds sexual. Say Me entusiasma mucho el proyecto.

Many of these phrases also work in person; see {{link:talking-to-coworkers-in-spanish|talking to coworkers in Spanish}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish for online meetings comes down to a handful of reliable phrases: check the audio, take turns politely, confirm next steps and close warmly. Prepare them once and every call gets easier. For more workplace and everyday moments, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you start an online meeting in Spanish?
faq.a: Greet everyone with Buenos días a todos, check the audio with ¿Me escuchan bien? and state the goal with El objetivo de hoy es…

faq.q: How do you say “You’re on mute” in Spanish?
faq.a: Estás en silencio or Tienes el micrófono apagado.

faq.q: Is it okay to use English tech words in Spanish meetings?
faq.a: In relaxed teams, words like link and mute are common. In formal meetings, use the Spanish terms.

faq.q: How do you end a meeting politely in Spanish?
faq.a: Summarize, confirm next steps and close with Gracias a todos por su tiempo. Que tengan buen día.
